pass1.confidenceBasis: Corroborating — exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed -1.27% YoY vs control +1.27%, differential -2.54, +2.08 SD past the clean pre-2020 window and parked past its -2.48 line, as_of 2026-06), reabsorption headline (prime-age employment share 80.2, 12m change -0.5 at +1.77 SD, decomposition shows employment itself down -1.38%, as_of 2026-06) plus its long-term-unemployed readout (27.3%, +4.0 in 12m), with ai_adoption (21.7% of firms and rising, 38.8% at 250+ employees, as_of 2026-07) opening the deployment gate; failing to corroborate or refuting — job_postings_spread (6-month change +2.6, i.e. the earliest and occupation-cut panel is easing, as_of 2026-07), reabsorption's own layoffs_rate (1.1, -0.1 over 12m, below norm: frozen not shedding) and hires_minus_quits (1.4, +0.1 over 12m), exposed_vs_control_wages (+1.11 in favour of exposed, though its own weighting rule disqualifies it while exposed employment falls), labor_productivity (2.8%, in the internet-boom band, as_of 2026-03); all three doubts are unmet — the entire 12-month EPOP decline sits inside the last 3 months (3m change also -0.5), the independent establishment source is economy-wide positive (+57k payrolls, 4.2% unemployment) against the household survey's fall, and the leading postings panel is pointing the other way.

falsifier.unit: percentage points (12-month change in the 25-54 employment-population ratio)

pass1.falsifierPlain: The prime-age employment-share chart moves first: if it climbs back to flat or better year-over-year while the long-term-unemployed share falls back to 25% or less, the aggregate market is catching exits again and this displacement reading was wrong.
pass1.reasoningLog:
**What I am claiming, plainly.** This is not "displacement not started" being dressed up, and it is not resting on absence of deterioration. It rests on observed deterioration: the household survey's prime-age employment share is down 0.5 points over twelve months at +1.77 SD against the clean pre-2020 window, past this panel's own registered 1-SD deterioration line, and the decomposition says employment itself is down 1.4 million (-1.38%) rather than the population having grown. Paired with an exposed-industry job growth rate that is outright negative (-1.27% YoY) while controls run +1.27%, that is the combination the dashboard's own logic reserves for displacement rather than reallocation: something specific to exposed work, and the aggregate has not caught the outflow. The confidence is LOW because almost all of the absorption movement is one quarter old, the leading panel is improving, and the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey economy-wide.

**exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).** Name the sides: exposed industries are contracting at -1.27% YoY; controls are expanding at +1.27%. The differential -2.54 sits past the -2.48 attribution line and +2.08 SD past the fixed 2010-2019 window (I am reasoning from the fixed window, per the divergence note — full history puts it at only +0.75 because the period under test has been absorbed into "normal"). The panel role binds: this establishes that something is specific to AI-exposed work, not that work was destroyed. Perfect reallocation would produce exactly this reading. So on its own it does nothing but license the question.

*Inversion.* The strongest opposite reading: this gap's full-history trough was -5.22 in November 2023, so it has *narrowed by 2.7 points* while firm AI adoption climbed from 17.3% to 21.7%. A divergence that peaked before the tools diffused and has been shrinking since looks like the 2021-22 hiring correction decaying, not an AI signal ramping. The gap is also flat over the last four readings — the "2 consecutive readings past the alarm line spanning 1 month" is a level parked past a line, not a fresh widening. And half the gap is the *control* side being strong: if the exposed outflow went into construction, health and leisure, this panel's maximally negative reading is what benign job-switching looks like. Finally the industry proxy is crude — a janitor in the information sector counts as exposed, a data analyst in manufacturing does not.

*Residual after the hiring correction.* The correction explains the shape and much of the magnitude of 2023-24. What it explains less well four years on is exposed employment being *negative in level* in mid-2026 with controls healthy, a curve that is not inverted, and adoption rising. That residual is what I am reading, and it is thin.

**reabsorption (REABSORPTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).** The reading rule binds: the headline 12-month change places the axis; the four secondary readouts are context; the 3-month figures are context at one further remove.

- Headline: 80.2%, -0.5 over 12 months, deviation +1.77 (fixed window; the two baselines agree here, so this does not depend on the window). That is past the panel's registered deterioration threshold of 1 SD. Direction: falling. Level: 0.25 points *above* 2019, which is the panel's own reminder that the level is slow to register a fresh turn from a high start.
- Decomposition: employed -1,436k (-1.38%), population -952k. Per the caveat I discount the population leg hardest and do not quote its size — the January 2026 control revision put a ~-1.5M level shift into it. What the decomposition *does* settle is the direction question: employment is falling, so the ratio is not falling merely because more people arrived. That is the single most load-bearing fact in this reading.
- Long-term unemployed share 27.3%, +4.0 over 12 months, deviation +0.96 (just shy of the attention line). Rising, and 3-month +1.9 agrees. Exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.
- Underemployment gap 3.7, +0.1 over 12 months, deviation +1.48 on the fixed window (past attention). Small in level terms; the 3-month is flat and disagrees with the 12-month, so I treat this as weak.
- Layoffs 1.1, -0.1 over 12 months, deviation -0.34, i.e. *below* norm and falling. Paired with a hires rate of 3.4 against quits 2.0, the panel's own pairing rule says this is a FROZEN market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, the burden is on entrants and on people who have already left. That materially changes the character of the story. If AI is removing work here it is doing it through the hiring channel, not through layoffs, and a frozen market can produce a falling employment share with nobody being fired.
- Hires minus quits 1.4, +0.1 over 12 months, deviation -0.9, i.e. further *away* from displacement. Name the moving side: the net improved because quits fell to 2.0, not because hiring is strong — a 3.4 hires rate is low by 2010s standards. A net figure improving on falling quits is a frozen market again, not absorption.

*Inversion of the reabsorption panel.* The best opposite case is strong. (i) The whole 12-month decline is inside the last quarter: 12m change -0.5 and 3m change -0.5 are the same number, so this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it, in a survey whose response rates degraded through late 2025 and which lost October 2025 entirely on the companion tracker. (ii) The level is still above 2019. (iii) Layoffs below norm and net hiring up are what a market that is *not* removing people looks like. (iv) Economy-wide, payrolls are +57k and unemployment is 4.2% — I flag explicitly that those are economy-wide CES/CPS headline figures and cannot be used as evidence about exposed industries, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the *aggregate* is failing to absorb, which is precisely what this panel is for. Three of the readouts I lean on (headline, long-term share, U6-U3) are the same household survey, so their agreement is weaker than it looks.

I considered whether the population-control revision could be manufacturing the headline fall and therefore the whole verdict. The panel asserts employment is seasonally adjusted and does not carry the same discontinuity, and that the ratio is computed consistently within a control regime. I am not fully persuaded — CPS employment *levels* are reweighted by the same controls, and the -1,436k employment change is suspiciously close in magnitude to the stated ~-1.5M January control shift. I am recording that as the single largest fragility in this reading rather than as a confounder, because the published *ratio* is the measure the panel says to trust and it fell on both horizons.

**exposed_vs_control_wages (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06).** Exposed pay +4.63% YoY, control +3.53%, differential +1.11, deviation -0.82 (further *away* from displacement), 23 consecutive readings inside its 2010s range. The weighting rule binds and disqualifies this from being strong support for either side, because exposed employment is falling (-1.27%): if entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped, the survivors skew senior and the average rises with nobody getting a raise. Note also the one-month jump from +0.71 (May) to +1.11 (June) against a panel described as flat over four readings — that looks like noise and I would not build anything on it. Composition question: unresolved, and it weakens the panel. This is the *only* exposed-specific candidate for positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, and it cannot carry that weight — which is the main reason I did not read AUGMENTATION.

**individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, as_of 2026-06).** Stayers 3.6, switchers 4.4, premium 0.8, deviation -0.54 (away from displacement), recovering over the last four readings. Economy-wide, so it can never attribute anything to exposed work. Its job is the cross-check: it is *not* flat-or-falling while the industry average accelerates, so the crude "the acceleration is pure composition" story is not confirmed either. That leaves the composition question genuinely unresolved rather than resolved in my favour, and I have treated it that way. Substantively, a positive switcher premium is the cleanest single piece of evidence against my verdict: people who move jobs are still landing better than people who stay, which is opportunity-driven mobility, not distress mobility. It is economy-wide, and it is a median, so a collapse concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly the shape it would miss.

**job_postings_spread (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old — the freshest attribution panel).** Sides named: exposed knowledge-work postings 76.9, i.e. 23.1% *below* their own February 2020 level; control hands-on postings 105.3, i.e. 5.3% *above* theirs. Per the weighting rule I read the change, not the level: spread_change_over_6_months is +2.6, meaning the gap has *narrowed* over six months, and the current -28.4 is narrower than its own 2023-2026 mean of -33.5 (deviation -1.17, away from displacement). No usable pre-2020 baseline, no threshold, and its level is substantially a 2022 rates event still sitting there. So this panel cuts *against* my verdict on the only dimension it is allowed to speak on. It is the leading indicator and it is the freshest attribution reading I have, and I am reading displacement anyway — that is the largest single reason this is LOW and not MEDIUM. Against it: postings easing by 2.6 index points over six months from -28.4 is a modest move on a series whose own history spans -42.8 to -21.4, and it is an advertised intention, not a filled job. The month-over-month move flagged in what_changed (-28.1 to -28.4, same reading date 2026-07, so a revision rather than a new observation) is trivial and I give it no weight.

**labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, as_of 2026-03, 5 months old).** 2.8% YoY, up from 2.5%, inside the 2.7-3.4 internet-boom band for one quarter, roughly +1.4 SD above the pre-2020 mean of 1.27. Economy-wide, heavily revised, and it cannot attribute anything to AI. Read as the role instructs: gains *are* visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like — and it is the strongest thing on this dashboard pointing at augmentation. It does not reach the two-quarters-above-3.4 break. Vintage gap: this is 5 months older than the attribution and reabsorption panels, so the counterweight to my verdict on the gains side cannot yet reflect a recent turn; but note the asymmetry runs the *other* way here too, in that the evidence arguing against me (postings, 2026-07) is in one case *newer* than the evidence supporting me (jobs and reabsorption, 2026-06). I am stating that plainly: my freshest panel disagrees with me.

**worker_share_of_income (DESCRIPTIVE, no vote, as_of 2026-03).** 51.0%, four consecutive quarterly declines, -0.96 over four quarters against a forty-year drift of -0.13/year, in the fastest 10% of declines on record and at the bottom of its full history. I am not counting this, per the panel role, and correctly so: ordinary recessions produced -2.18 and -1.59. But it is worth recording that labour's share is falling at roughly seven times the secular pace in the same quarter that productivity printed 2.8%. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story would have, and this panel is barred from voting on it. Economy-wide either way.

**ai_adoption (DEPLOYMENT_GATE, as_of 2026-07).** 21.7% of firms, monotone-ish from 17.3% in November 2025, and a size gradient of 1.87 (38.8% at 250+ employees vs 20.8% at 1-4), so worker exposure exceeds the firm share. The gate is open: a displacement reading is permitted. It causes nothing. I list it as load-bearing only in the sense that without it the word "AI" could not attach to the reading at all. *Inversion:* adoption of a tool in "any business function" is a very low bar — it includes a marketing team using a chatbot — and rising adoption alongside a *narrowing* exposed-vs-control gap since 2023 is arguably evidence against the causal link.

**Panels that contribute nothing, read anyway.** ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation is 11 months stale and essentially unchanged across three releases (43.1/56.9); I note only that the split has been stable, and it measures one vendor's conversations, not jobs. ai_capability_metr (as_of 2026-04) shows an 80% horizon of 186 minutes for the leading model, a large jump over the field; ai_capability_gdpval_ratings has Anthropic leading OpenAI by ~125 Elo; ai_capability_vs_human_experts shows 70.9% wins-plus-ties but 49.7% wins-only, i.e. just under true parity, self-reported, and nothing published since December 2025. Interesting, and counted in nothing: a model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert, and none of these can corroborate a labor reading in either direction. I have not used them.

**Macro / cyclical test.** macro_regime (as_of 2026-08): curve +0.5 and not inverted, real 10-year 2.5%, expected inflation 2.3%. Per the role, this can name the cyclical hypothesis and can never clear it, and I have not used it to exculpate anything. The contemporaneous test is the one that matters, and I ran it on the controls: control industry jobs +1.27% YoY, control pay +3.53%, control postings 5.3% *above* their own February 2020 level, layoffs economy-wide at 1.1 and falling. A general macro contraction would have pulled the control side down with the exposed side, and it has not. That cuts in my favour. Where it cuts against me: the *aggregate* reabsorption weakness I am leaning on is economy-wide, and if the exposed side alone is weak then a falling economy-wide prime-age employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either an artefact (see the population-control worry) or a genuine broad softening that the controls are not showing. That tension is unresolved and it is a real hole in my reading, not a rhetorical concession.

**Why not CONFOUNDED.** I can name candidate causes — the 2021-22 hiring correction, the 2022 rate shock still sitting in the postings level, and the January 2026 Census population-control revision. The first two are weighed against my reading, not alongside it, and neither is a live 2026 event: the correction's peak effect was the -5.22 gap in late 2023 and the postings spread has been flat since 2022, so both are decaying, not driving. The third is the closest to a genuine confounder and it has a series behind it (decomposition.population_change_thousands -952, with a stated ~-1.5M control shift), but the panel states the published ratio is computed consistently within a control regime and it is the ratio that fell on both horizons. Mixed evidence is not grounds for CONFOUNDED, so I take the directional reading and put the weakness in the rating.

**News.** BLS Employment Situation through 2026-06: payrolls 158,984k, +57k on the month, unemployment 4.2%. That is economy-wide establishment data and I do not pair it with exposed-industry figures; it is legitimate counterweight to the household survey's absorption failure, and I have counted it as such. +57k is soft but positive, and 4.2% is not a market removing work at scale. The AP items reference an Iran war, inflation, the Fed and mortgages. An energy or conflict shock could move hiring, but it would show up in controls too — construction and leisure are more rate- and energy-sensitive than information services — and both are strong; it is also too recent to sit inside June data, and it does not explain why exposed-industry *pay* is running 1.1 points ahead of control. The mortgage/Fed thread is the one worth flagging: rate-sensitive white-collar hiring is exactly the 2022 mechanism the postings panel attributes its level to, so if rates are again the story, the postings spread should be *widening* — it is narrowing (+2.6 over six months), so I set that hypothesis aside. The "job openings" item is JOLTS commentary and the JOLTS series themselves are in the panel (hires 3.4, quits 2.0, layoffs 1.1); the series, not the coverage, is what I read. No news item in this package attributes headcount decisions to AI, so I have no employer-incentive-contaminated claim to discount this run. News generated hypotheses and moved nothing.

**Overturn design.** My verdict is displacement, so the overturn condition must be the labour market absorbing people again. Primary: reabsorption headline.change_over_12_months at_or_above 0.0. Current -0.5; pre-2020 SD of 12-month changes is 0.52 and the pre-2020 mean is +0.42, so 0.0 is well inside one SD of normal and the series demonstrably traversed 0.5 points in the last single quarter, which is why I judge it reachable inside 90 days. It is monthly and publishes three more times before 2026-11-02, so the window cannot close without observations — unlike the quarterly productivity and income-share panels, where a 90-day test could see literally nothing new. Discrimination check: what else carries this to ≥0.0? An ordinary rebound would, but an ordinary rebound *is* my reading being wrong, since my reading is built on this series falling. A January population-control revision cannot land before November. A seasonal artefact cannot, because this is a 12-month change on a seasonally adjusted series. Secondary, to stop a single noisy print from overturning and to require that people are actually landing: secondary.long_term_unemployed_share.latest_value at_or_below 25.0, against 27.3 now and a 12-month rise of 4.0 with a 12-month SD of 5.2, so a 2.3-point retracement is well inside this series' demonstrated volatility. Both must hold. I considered using hires_minus_quits or layoffs_rate as the second condition and rejected both: they already read *away* from displacement (-0.9 and -0.34 deviation), so a threshold there would be tripped by the status quo and would discriminate nothing — the same error as setting a trigger at a level a known confounder already reached. I also considered requiring the exposed-vs-control differential to heal above -2.2, but that measures reallocation, not absorption, and my verdict turns on absorption; a healed gap with absorption still failing would not make me wrong in the way that matters.

**What would make me wrong in a way this test would not catch:** if the household survey's prime-age fall turns out to be a weighting artefact that is silently revised rather than reversed in the published 12-month change. I cannot construct a mechanical guard against that from these panels, and I am recording it here so a later run can hold me to it.

VERDICT: DISPLACEMENT
CONFIDENCE: LOW
CONFIDENCE_BASIS: Corroborating — exposed_vs_control_jobs (exposed -1.27% YoY vs control +1.27%, differential -2.54, +2.08 SD past the clean pre-2020 window and parked past its -2.48 line, as_of 2026-06), reabsorption headline (prime-age employment share 80.2, 12m change -0.5 at +1.77 SD, decomposition shows employment itself down -1.38%, as_of 2026-06) plus its long-term-unemployed readout (27.3%, +4.0 in 12m), with ai_adoption (21.7% of firms and rising, 38.8% at 250+ employees, as_of 2026-07) opening the deployment gate; failing to corroborate or refuting — job_postings_spread (6-month change +2.6, i.e. the earliest and occupation-cut panel is easing, as_of 2026-07), reabsorption's own layoffs_rate (1.1, -0.1 over 12m, below norm: frozen not shedding) and hires_minus_quits (1.4, +0.1 over 12m), exposed_vs_control_wages (+1.11 in favour of exposed, though its own weighting rule disqualifies it while exposed employment falls), labor_productivity (2.8%, in the internet-boom band, as_of 2026-03); all three doubts are unmet — the entire 12-month EPOP decline sits inside the last 3 months (3m change also -0.5), the independent establishment source is economy-wide positive (+57k payrolls, 4.2% unemployment) against the household survey's fall, and the leading postings panel is pointing the other way.
LOAD_BEARING_PANELS: reabsorption, exposed_vs_control_jobs, ai_adoption
CONFOUNDER: NONE
OVERTURN_PANEL: reabsorption
OVERTURN_FIELD: headline.change_over_12_months
OVERTURN_COMPARATOR: at_or_above
OVERTURN_VALUE: 0.0
OVERTURN_UNIT: percentage points (12-month change in the 25-54 employment-population ratio)
OVERTURN_ALSO_PANEL: reabsorption
OVERTURN_ALSO_FIELD: secondary.long_term_unemployed_share.latest_value
OVERTURN_ALSO_COMPARATOR: at_or_below
OVERTURN_ALSO_VALUE: 25.0
OVERTURN_BY: 2026-11-02
OVERTURN_PLAIN: The prime-age employment-share chart moves first: if it climbs back to flat or better year-over-year while the long-term-unemployed share falls back to 25% or less, the aggregate market is catching exits again and this displacement reading was wrong.

REASONING_LOG:

**What I am claiming, plainly.** This is not "displacement not started" being dressed up, and it is not resting on absence of deterioration. It rests on observed deterioration: the household survey's prime-age employment share is down 0.5 points over twelve months at +1.77 SD against the clean pre-2020 window, past this panel's own registered 1-SD deterioration line, and the decomposition says employment itself is down 1.4 million (-1.38%) rather than the population having grown. Paired with an exposed-industry job growth rate that is outright negative (-1.27% YoY) while controls run +1.27%, that is the combination the dashboard's own logic reserves for displacement rather than reallocation: something specific to exposed work, and the aggregate has not caught the outflow. The confidence is LOW because almost all of the absorption movement is one quarter old, the leading panel is improving, and the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey economy-wide.

**exposed_vs_control_jobs (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).** Name the sides: exposed industries are contracting at -1.27% YoY; controls are expanding at +1.27%. The differential -2.54 sits past the -2.48 attribution line and +2.08 SD past the fixed 2010-2019 window (I am reasoning from the fixed window, per the divergence note — full history puts it at only +0.75 because the period under test has been absorbed into "normal"). The panel role binds: this establishes that something is specific to AI-exposed work, not that work was destroyed. Perfect reallocation would produce exactly this reading. So on its own it does nothing but license the question.

*Inversion.* The strongest opposite reading: this gap's full-history trough was -5.22 in November 2023, so it has *narrowed by 2.7 points* while firm AI adoption climbed from 17.3% to 21.7%. A divergence that peaked before the tools diffused and has been shrinking since looks like the 2021-22 hiring correction decaying, not an AI signal ramping. The gap is also flat over the last four readings — the "2 consecutive readings past the alarm line spanning 1 month" is a level parked past a line, not a fresh widening. And half the gap is the *control* side being strong: if the exposed outflow went into construction, health and leisure, this panel's maximally negative reading is what benign job-switching looks like. Finally the industry proxy is crude — a janitor in the information sector counts as exposed, a data analyst in manufacturing does not.

*Residual after the hiring correction.* The correction explains the shape and much of the magnitude of 2023-24. What it explains less well four years on is exposed employment being *negative in level* in mid-2026 with controls healthy, a curve that is not inverted, and adoption rising. That residual is what I am reading, and it is thin.

**reabsorption (REABSORPTION, as_of 2026-06, 2 months old).** The reading rule binds: the headline 12-month change places the axis; the four secondary readouts are context; the 3-month figures are context at one further remove.

- Headline: 80.2%, -0.5 over 12 months, deviation +1.77 (fixed window; the two baselines agree here, so this does not depend on the window). That is past the panel's registered deterioration threshold of 1 SD. Direction: falling. Level: 0.25 points *above* 2019, which is the panel's own reminder that the level is slow to register a fresh turn from a high start.
- Decomposition: employed -1,436k (-1.38%), population -952k. Per the caveat I discount the population leg hardest and do not quote its size — the January 2026 control revision put a ~-1.5M level shift into it. What the decomposition *does* settle is the direction question: employment is falling, so the ratio is not falling merely because more people arrived. That is the single most load-bearing fact in this reading.
- Long-term unemployed share 27.3%, +4.0 over 12 months, deviation +0.96 (just shy of the attention line). Rising, and 3-month +1.9 agrees. Exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.
- Underemployment gap 3.7, +0.1 over 12 months, deviation +1.48 on the fixed window (past attention). Small in level terms; the 3-month is flat and disagrees with the 12-month, so I treat this as weak.
- Layoffs 1.1, -0.1 over 12 months, deviation -0.34, i.e. *below* norm and falling. Paired with a hires rate of 3.4 against quits 2.0, the panel's own pairing rule says this is a FROZEN market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, the burden is on entrants and on people who have already left. That materially changes the character of the story. If AI is removing work here it is doing it through the hiring channel, not through layoffs, and a frozen market can produce a falling employment share with nobody being fired.
- Hires minus quits 1.4, +0.1 over 12 months, deviation -0.9, i.e. further *away* from displacement. Name the moving side: the net improved because quits fell to 2.0, not because hiring is strong — a 3.4 hires rate is low by 2010s standards. A net figure improving on falling quits is a frozen market again, not absorption.

*Inversion of the reabsorption panel.* The best opposite case is strong. (i) The whole 12-month decline is inside the last quarter: 12m change -0.5 and 3m change -0.5 are the same number, so this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it, in a survey whose response rates degraded through late 2025 and which lost October 2025 entirely on the companion tracker. (ii) The level is still above 2019. (iii) Layoffs below norm and net hiring up are what a market that is *not* removing people looks like. (iv) Economy-wide, payrolls are +57k and unemployment is 4.2% — I flag explicitly that those are economy-wide CES/CPS headline figures and cannot be used as evidence about exposed industries, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the *aggregate* is failing to absorb, which is precisely what this panel is for. Three of the readouts I lean on (headline, long-term share, U6-U3) are the same household survey, so their agreement is weaker than it looks.

I considered whether the population-control revision could be manufacturing the headline fall and therefore the whole verdict. The panel asserts employment is seasonally adjusted and does not carry the same discontinuity, and that the ratio is computed consistently within a control regime. I am not fully persuaded — CPS employment *levels* are reweighted by the same controls, and the -1,436k employment change is suspiciously close in magnitude to the stated ~-1.5M January control shift. I am recording that as the single largest fragility in this reading rather than as a confounder, because the published *ratio* is the measure the panel says to trust and it fell on both horizons.

**exposed_vs_control_wages (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-06).** Exposed pay +4.63% YoY, control +3.53%, differential +1.11, deviation -0.82 (further *away* from displacement), 23 consecutive readings inside its 2010s range. The weighting rule binds and disqualifies this from being strong support for either side, because exposed employment is falling (-1.27%): if entry-level hiring in exposed industries has stopped, the survivors skew senior and the average rises with nobody getting a raise. Note also the one-month jump from +0.71 (May) to +1.11 (June) against a panel described as flat over four readings — that looks like noise and I would not build anything on it. Composition question: unresolved, and it weakens the panel. This is the *only* exposed-specific candidate for positive evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, and it cannot carry that weight — which is the main reason I did not read AUGMENTATION.

**individual_wage_growth (COMPOSITION_CONTROL, as_of 2026-06).** Stayers 3.6, switchers 4.4, premium 0.8, deviation -0.54 (away from displacement), recovering over the last four readings. Economy-wide, so it can never attribute anything to exposed work. Its job is the cross-check: it is *not* flat-or-falling while the industry average accelerates, so the crude "the acceleration is pure composition" story is not confirmed either. That leaves the composition question genuinely unresolved rather than resolved in my favour, and I have treated it that way. Substantively, a positive switcher premium is the cleanest single piece of evidence against my verdict: people who move jobs are still landing better than people who stay, which is opportunity-driven mobility, not distress mobility. It is economy-wide, and it is a median, so a collapse concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly the shape it would miss.

**job_postings_spread (ATTRIBUTION, as_of 2026-07, 1 month old — the freshest attribution panel).** Sides named: exposed knowledge-work postings 76.9, i.e. 23.1% *below* their own February 2020 level; control hands-on postings 105.3, i.e. 5.3% *above* theirs. Per the weighting rule I read the change, not the level: spread_change_over_6_months is +2.6, meaning the gap has *narrowed* over six months, and the current -28.4 is narrower than its own 2023-2026 mean of -33.5 (deviation -1.17, away from displacement). No usable pre-2020 baseline, no threshold, and its level is substantially a 2022 rates event still sitting there. So this panel cuts *against* my verdict on the only dimension it is allowed to speak on. It is the leading indicator and it is the freshest attribution reading I have, and I am reading displacement anyway — that is the largest single reason this is LOW and not MEDIUM. Against it: postings easing by 2.6 index points over six months from -28.4 is a modest move on a series whose own history spans -42.8 to -21.4, and it is an advertised intention, not a filled job. The month-over-month move flagged in what_changed (-28.1 to -28.4, same reading date 2026-07, so a revision rather than a new observation) is trivial and I give it no weight.

**labor_productivity (GAINS_TEST, as_of 2026-03, 5 months old).** 2.8% YoY, up from 2.5%, inside the 2.7-3.4 internet-boom band for one quarter, roughly +1.4 SD above the pre-2020 mean of 1.27. Economy-wide, heavily revised, and it cannot attribute anything to AI. Read as the role instructs: gains *are* visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like — and it is the strongest thing on this dashboard pointing at augmentation. It does not reach the two-quarters-above-3.4 break. Vintage gap: this is 5 months older than the attribution and reabsorption panels, so the counterweight to my verdict on the gains side cannot yet reflect a recent turn; but note the asymmetry runs the *other* way here too, in that the evidence arguing against me (postings, 2026-07) is in one case *newer* than the evidence supporting me (jobs and reabsorption, 2026-06). I am stating that plainly: my freshest panel disagrees with me.

**worker_share_of_income (DESCRIPTIVE, no vote, as_of 2026-03).** 51.0%, four consecutive quarterly declines, -0.96 over four quarters against a forty-year drift of -0.13/year, in the fastest 10% of declines on record and at the bottom of its full history. I am not counting this, per the panel role, and correctly so: ordinary recessions produced -2.18 and -1.59. But it is worth recording that labour's share is falling at roughly seven times the secular pace in the same quarter that productivity printed 2.8%. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story would have, and this panel is barred from voting on it. Economy-wide either way.

**ai_adoption (DEPLOYMENT_GATE, as_of 2026-07).** 21.7% of firms, monotone-ish from 17.3% in November 2025, and a size gradient of 1.87 (38.8% at 250+ employees vs 20.8% at 1-4), so worker exposure exceeds the firm share. The gate is open: a displacement reading is permitted. It causes nothing. I list it as load-bearing only in the sense that without it the word "AI" could not attach to the reading at all. *Inversion:* adoption of a tool in "any business function" is a very low bar — it includes a marketing team using a chatbot — and rising adoption alongside a *narrowing* exposed-vs-control gap since 2023 is arguably evidence against the causal link.

**Panels that contribute nothing, read anyway.** ai_use_automation_vs_augmentation is 11 months stale and essentially unchanged across three releases (43.1/56.9); I note only that the split has been stable, and it measures one vendor's conversations, not jobs. ai_capability_metr (as_of 2026-04) shows an 80% horizon of 186 minutes for the leading model, a large jump over the field; ai_capability_gdpval_ratings has Anthropic leading OpenAI by ~125 Elo; ai_capability_vs_human_experts shows 70.9% wins-plus-ties but 49.7% wins-only, i.e. just under true parity, self-reported, and nothing published since December 2025. Interesting, and counted in nothing: a model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert, and none of these can corroborate a labor reading in either direction. I have not used them.

**Macro / cyclical test.** macro_regime (as_of 2026-08): curve +0.5 and not inverted, real 10-year 2.5%, expected inflation 2.3%. Per the role, this can name the cyclical hypothesis and can never clear it, and I have not used it to exculpate anything. The contemporaneous test is the one that matters, and I ran it on the controls: control industry jobs +1.27% YoY, control pay +3.53%, control postings 5.3% *above* their own February 2020 level, layoffs economy-wide at 1.1 and falling. A general macro contraction would have pulled the control side down with the exposed side, and it has not. That cuts in my favour. Where it cuts against me: the *aggregate* reabsorption weakness I am leaning on is economy-wide, and if the exposed side alone is weak then a falling economy-wide prime-age employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either an artefact (see the population-control worry) or a genuine broad softening that the controls are not showing. That tension is unresolved and it is a real hole in my reading, not a rhetorical concession.

**Why not CONFOUNDED.** I can name candidate causes — the 2021-22 hiring correction, the 2022 rate shock still sitting in the postings level, and the January 2026 Census population-control revision. The first two are weighed against my reading, not alongside it, and neither is a live 2026 event: the correction's peak effect was the -5.22 gap in late 2023 and the postings spread has been flat since 2022, so both are decaying, not driving. The third is the closest to a genuine confounder and it has a series behind it (decomposition.population_change_thousands -952, with a stated ~-1.5M control shift), but the panel states the published ratio is computed consistently within a control regime and it is the ratio that fell on both horizons. Mixed evidence is not grounds for CONFOUNDED, so I take the directional reading and put the weakness in the rating.

**News.** BLS Employment Situation through 2026-06: payrolls 158,984k, +57k on the month, unemployment 4.2%. That is economy-wide establishment data and I do not pair it with exposed-industry figures; it is legitimate counterweight to the household survey's absorption failure, and I have counted it as such. +57k is soft but positive, and 4.2% is not a market removing work at scale. The AP items reference an Iran war, inflation, the Fed and mortgages. An energy or conflict shock could move hiring, but it would show up in controls too — construction and leisure are more rate- and energy-sensitive than information services — and both are strong; it is also too recent to sit inside June data, and it does not explain why exposed-industry *pay* is running 1.1 points ahead of control. The mortgage/Fed thread is the one worth flagging: rate-sensitive white-collar hiring is exactly the 2022 mechanism the postings panel attributes its level to, so if rates are again the story, the postings spread should be *widening* — it is narrowing (+2.6 over six months), so I set that hypothesis aside. The "job openings" item is JOLTS commentary and the JOLTS series themselves are in the panel (hires 3.4, quits 2.0, layoffs 1.1); the series, not the coverage, is what I read. No news item in this package attributes headcount decisions to AI, so I have no employer-incentive-contaminated claim to discount this run. News generated hypotheses and moved nothing.

**Overturn design.** My verdict is displacement, so the overturn condition must be the labour market absorbing people again. Primary: reabsorption headline.change_over_12_months at_or_above 0.0. Current -0.5; pre-2020 SD of 12-month changes is 0.52 and the pre-2020 mean is +0.42, so 0.0 is well inside one SD of normal and the series demonstrably traversed 0.5 points in the last single quarter, which is why I judge it reachable inside 90 days. It is monthly and publishes three more times before 2026-11-02, so the window cannot close without observations — unlike the quarterly productivity and income-share panels, where a 90-day test could see literally nothing new. Discrimination check: what else carries this to ≥0.0? An ordinary rebound would, but an ordinary rebound *is* my reading being wrong, since my reading is built on this series falling. A January population-control revision cannot land before November. A seasonal artefact cannot, because this is a 12-month change on a seasonally adjusted series. Secondary, to stop a single noisy print from overturning and to require that people are actually landing: secondary.long_term_unemployed_share.latest_value at_or_below 25.0, against 27.3 now and a 12-month rise of 4.0 with a 12-month SD of 5.2, so a 2.3-point retracement is well inside this series' demonstrated volatility. Both must hold. I considered using hires_minus_quits or layoffs_rate as the second condition and rejected both: they already read *away* from displacement (-0.9 and -0.34 deviation), so a threshold there would be tripped by the status quo and would discriminate nothing — the same error as setting a trigger at a level a known confounder already reached. I also considered requiring the exposed-vs-control differential to heal above -2.2, but that measures reallocation, not absorption, and my verdict turns on absorption; a healed gap with absorption still failing would not make me wrong in the way that matters.

**What would make me wrong in a way this test would not catch:** if the household survey's prime-age fall turns out to be a weighting artefact that is silently revised rather than reversed in the published 12-month change. I cannot construct a mechanical guard against that from these panels, and I am recording it here so a later run can hold me to it.

pass2.notificationLine: Nothing new this month; displacement holds on prime-age employment down 0.5 points
pass2.publishedNote:
The reading is displacement, held with low confidence, and it rests on deterioration that has actually shown up in the data rather than on an absence of good news.

Nothing moved this month. One of thirteen panels changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. Everything below is last month's evidence read again.

What supports the displacement reading: employment in the industries most exposed to AI is shrinking, down 1.27% over the year, while industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. Meanwhile the share of 25-to-54-year-olds with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and that fall comes from employment dropping by about 1.4 million rather than from a bigger population. A specific slice of the economy losing work while the wider market fails to absorb the outflow is what separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling. The mechanism is a hiring freeze, not firing: layoffs are low at 1.1 and falling, hiring is weak at 3.4, and 27.3% of the unemployed have now been out of work more than six months, up four points in a year. The cost is landing on people trying to get in and people already out.

What argues against it, and this is where the low confidence comes from: the freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees. Job postings lead everything else here, and the shortfall in postings for exposed knowledge work — currently about 23% below its February 2020 level, against hands-on work sitting about 5% above its own — has been closing over the past six months, not widening. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 interest-rate shock. On a longer view the exposed-industry job shortfall was worse in late 2023, before AI tools diffused widely, and has narrowed while firm adoption climbed from 17.3% to 21.7% since November. A signal loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction unwinding. Pay also runs the wrong way for displacement: exposed industries are paying 4.63% growth against 3.53% in control industries, though that could simply be entry-level hiring stopping and the remaining workforce skewing senior. Economy-wide, job switchers still earn 4.4% growth against 3.6% for stayers, which is opportunity-driven mobility, not distress — that figure covers the whole workforce, not exposed industries, so distress concentrated among a minority is exactly what it would miss. Productivity at 2.8% a year, against a pre-2020 norm near 1.3%, is the strongest sign pointing at augmentation, and it too is economy-wide.

One thing readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed: it may not be trustworthy. The entire twelve-month fall happened inside the most recent quarter, and the January population-control revision pushed a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey — close to the 1.4 million employment drop doing the work here. The published ratio is meant to be consistent within a control regime and fell on both the quarterly and annual views, which is why I have not called this a confounder. But if that fall is revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. Separately, payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%, both economy-wide, and neither looks like a market removing work at scale.

Watch the prime-age employment share chart. If it climbs back to flat or better against a year earlier, the market is catching exits again and this reading was wrong.
pass2.fullAnalysis:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence.

It matters what that rests on. This is not a case of saying displacement has not started and there is nothing to see; the reading rests on deterioration that has actually been observed in the data, not on the absence of good news. Two things are happening at once. Job growth in the industries most exposed to AI is negative: employment in those industries is down 1.27% over the past year, while the comparison industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. And the wider labour market is not visibly catching the people leaving: the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and the drop comes from employment falling by about 1.4 million rather than from population growth. When a specific slice of the economy is shedding work and the aggregate is not soaking it up, that is the combination that separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling.

Nothing moved this month. Of the thirteen panels, one changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. The industry job counts, the household employment survey, the pay series, productivity, adoption and the capability benchmarks are all exactly where they were. So this month adds no evidence in either direction, and everything below is the same body of evidence read again.

The character of the exposed-industry weakness is worth spelling out, because it is not mass firing. The layoff rate is 1.1 and falling, below its own normal range. Hiring is weak at 3.4, and quits are down to 2.0. That is a frozen market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, and the cost is falling on people trying to get in and on people who have already left. A market like that can produce a falling employment share with almost nobody being fired. If AI is removing work here, it is doing it through the hiring door rather than the exit door, and that shape also explains why the long-term unemployed share has climbed to 27.3% of the jobless, up four points in a year: exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.

Now the case against, which is strong enough that it holds the confidence down to low.

The freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees with the displacement reading. Job postings are the leading indicator here, and they are improving. Postings for exposed knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on control work sit about 5% above theirs, which looks damning until you read the direction rather than the level: the shortfall in knowledge-work postings has been closing over the past six months, not widening, and the current gap is narrower than its own average since 2023. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 rate shock rather than anything to do with AI. Postings data is one month newer than the industry job counts I am leaning on. So the newest thing I have argues against the verdict I have written, and I am saying so rather than burying it.

The same is true across a longer horizon. The gap between exposed and control industry job growth was far worse in late 2023 than it is now — the exposed side was contracting relative to controls by more than five points then, against two and a half now. That divergence peaked before AI tools diffused widely and has been shrinking while firm adoption rose from 17.3% of businesses last November to 21.7% now. A signal that was loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction decaying than like an AI effect ramping up. It is also worth noting that half of the current gap is the control side being genuinely strong: if the people leaving exposed industries walked into construction, health care and hospitality, this is what benign job-switching would look like on this chart.

Pay does not behave the way displacement usually does either. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing at 4.63% a year against 3.53% in the control industries. If AI were making these workers redundant, you would expect their pay to lag, not lead. But this cannot be taken as evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time: if entry-level hiring in those industries has stopped, the people left behind skew senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. I cannot separate those two stories with what is here, which is the main reason I did not read this as augmentation. The one cross-check available is economy-wide, not exposed-specific: people who switch jobs are still getting 4.4% pay growth against 3.6% for those who stay. That premium is not collapsing, which is the single cleanest piece of evidence against the displacement reading — people are still moving jobs for opportunity rather than out of distress. It is a median across the whole workforce, so distress concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly what it would miss.

Productivity is running at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, against a pre-2020 norm closer to 1.3%. Gains are visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like, and this is the strongest thing here pointing that way. Two caveats: the figure is five months older than the labour panels, and it is economy-wide, so it cannot be attributed to AI or to exposed industries. Alongside it, labour's share of national income has fallen for four straight quarters to 51.0%, about a point over the year against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story has, though ordinary recessions have produced sharper falls in labour's share than this one.

The largest weakness in this reading is not any of the above; it is a data problem, and readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed it. All of the twelve-month fall in the prime-age employment share happened inside the most recent quarter — the twelve-month and three-month changes are the same half point. So this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it. Worse, the January 2026 Census population-control revision put a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey, and the fall in employment I am leaning on is about 1.4 million, uncomfortably close to that. The published ratio is meant to be computed consistently within a control regime, and it fell on both the twelve-month and three-month views, which is why I have treated the revision as a fragility rather than as an outright alternative explanation. But I am not fully persuaded, and if this fall is quietly revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. The household survey's response rates also degraded through late 2025. Three of the readouts I lean on come from that same survey, so their agreement with each other is worth less than it looks.

Two further tensions I have not resolved. First, the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey at the aggregate level: payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%. Those are economy-wide figures and cannot be used to say anything about exposed industries specifically, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the aggregate market is failing to absorb people, which is precisely the claim doing the work here. Second, if weakness is confined to exposed industries while control industries are healthy, then a falling economy-wide employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either a measurement artefact or a broad softening the control industries are not showing. That does not add up cleanly, and I would rather say so than paper over it.

On the cyclical alternative: the yield curve is not inverted, and more to the point, a general downturn would drag the control industries down with the exposed ones. It has not. Control industry jobs, pay and postings are all healthy and layoffs are low, so a plain macro contraction does not fit. The rate-sensitivity story is the one worth watching — white-collar hiring is where the 2022 rate shock landed — but if rates were again the driver, the knowledge-work postings shortfall should be widening, and it is narrowing.

Finally, several panels that get talked about a lot contribute nothing here and I have not used them. AI systems now beat or tie human experts on about 71% of tested work tasks, and win outright just under half the time; the leading model can sustain tasks of roughly three hours at the measured reliability level. A model clearing an expert on a benchmark is not an employer deciding to stop paying that expert. TAGLINE: Nothing moved, freshest panel disagrees
FULL_ANALYSIS:
The reading is displacement, and it is held with low confidence.

It matters what that rests on. This is not a case of saying displacement has not started and there is nothing to see; the reading rests on deterioration that has actually been observed in the data, not on the absence of good news. Two things are happening at once. Job growth in the industries most exposed to AI is negative: employment in those industries is down 1.27% over the past year, while the comparison industries AI has barely touched are adding jobs at 1.27%. And the wider labour market is not visibly catching the people leaving: the share of Americans aged 25 to 54 with a job is 80.2%, down half a point over twelve months, and the drop comes from employment falling by about 1.4 million rather than from population growth. When a specific slice of the economy is shedding work and the aggregate is not soaking it up, that is the combination that separates displacement from ordinary reshuffling.

Nothing moved this month. Of the thirteen panels, one changed, and the change was a small downward revision to a job-postings figure already published for July, not a new observation. The industry job counts, the household employment survey, the pay series, productivity, adoption and the capability benchmarks are all exactly where they were. So this month adds no evidence in either direction, and everything below is the same body of evidence read again.

The character of the exposed-industry weakness is worth spelling out, because it is not mass firing. The layoff rate is 1.1 and falling, below its own normal range. Hiring is weak at 3.4, and quits are down to 2.0. That is a frozen market, not a shedding one: incumbents are not being pushed out, and the cost is falling on people trying to get in and on people who have already left. A market like that can produce a falling employment share with almost nobody being fired. If AI is removing work here, it is doing it through the hiring door rather than the exit door, and that shape also explains why the long-term unemployed share has climbed to 27.3% of the jobless, up four points in a year: exits are increasingly not being caught quickly.

Now the case against, which is strong enough that it holds the confidence down to low.

The freshest evidence on the dashboard disagrees with the displacement reading. Job postings are the leading indicator here, and they are improving. Postings for exposed knowledge work sit about 23% below their February 2020 level while postings for hands-on control work sit about 5% above theirs, which looks damning until you read the direction rather than the level: the shortfall in knowledge-work postings has been closing over the past six months, not widening, and the current gap is narrower than its own average since 2023. Much of that level is a hangover from the 2022 rate shock rather than anything to do with AI. Postings data is one month newer than the industry job counts I am leaning on. So the newest thing I have argues against the verdict I have written, and I am saying so rather than burying it.

The same is true across a longer horizon. The gap between exposed and control industry job growth was far worse in late 2023 than it is now — the exposed side was contracting relative to controls by more than five points then, against two and a half now. That divergence peaked before AI tools diffused widely and has been shrinking while firm adoption rose from 17.3% of businesses last November to 21.7% now. A signal that was loudest before the tools arrived looks more like the 2021-22 over-hiring correction decaying than like an AI effect ramping up. It is also worth noting that half of the current gap is the control side being genuinely strong: if the people leaving exposed industries walked into construction, health care and hospitality, this is what benign job-switching would look like on this chart.

Pay does not behave the way displacement usually does either. Pay in AI-exposed industries is growing at 4.63% a year against 3.53% in the control industries. If AI were making these workers redundant, you would expect their pay to lag, not lead. But this cannot be taken as evidence that exposed workers are being made more valuable, because exposed employment is shrinking at the same time: if entry-level hiring in those industries has stopped, the people left behind skew senior and the average wage rises without anyone getting a raise. I cannot separate those two stories with what is here, which is the main reason I did not read this as augmentation. The one cross-check available is economy-wide, not exposed-specific: people who switch jobs are still getting 4.4% pay growth against 3.6% for those who stay. That premium is not collapsing, which is the single cleanest piece of evidence against the displacement reading — people are still moving jobs for opportunity rather than out of distress. It is a median across the whole workforce, so distress concentrated in a minority of exposed workers is exactly what it would miss.

Productivity is running at 2.8% a year, up from 2.5%, against a pre-2020 norm closer to 1.3%. Gains are visible in the aggregate, which is what augmentation working would look like, and this is the strongest thing here pointing that way. Two caveats: the figure is five months older than the labour panels, and it is economy-wide, so it cannot be attributed to AI or to exposed industries. Alongside it, labour's share of national income has fallen for four straight quarters to 51.0%, about a point over the year against a long-run drift of roughly a tenth of a point a year. Productivity gains that do not reach workers is the shape a displacement story has, though ordinary recessions have produced sharper falls in labour's share than this one.

The largest weakness in this reading is not any of the above; it is a data problem, and readers relying on the prime-age employment figure are owed it. All of the twelve-month fall in the prime-age employment share happened inside the most recent quarter — the twelve-month and three-month changes are the same half point. So this is one quarter of evidence, not a year of it. Worse, the January 2026 Census population-control revision put a level shift of roughly 1.5 million into this survey, and the fall in employment I am leaning on is about 1.4 million, uncomfortably close to that. The published ratio is meant to be computed consistently within a control regime, and it fell on both the twelve-month and three-month views, which is why I have treated the revision as a fragility rather than as an outright alternative explanation. But I am not fully persuaded, and if this fall is quietly revised away rather than reversed, the displacement reading loses its load-bearing fact. The household survey's response rates also degraded through late 2025. Three of the readouts I lean on come from that same survey, so their agreement with each other is worth less than it looks.

Two further tensions I have not resolved. First, the establishment survey disagrees with the household survey at the aggregate level: payrolls rose 57,000 in June and unemployment is 4.2%. Those are economy-wide figures and cannot be used to say anything about exposed industries specifically, but they are legitimate evidence against the claim that the aggregate market is failing to absorb people, which is precisely the claim doing the work here. Second, if weakness is confined to exposed industries while control industries are healthy, then a falling economy-wide employment share needs a source outside exposed industries — which is either a measurement artefact or a broad softening the control industries are not showing. That does not add up cleanly, and I would rather say so than paper over it.

On the cyclical alternative: the yield curve is not inverted, and more to the point, a general downturn would drag the control industries down with the exposed ones. It has not. Control industry jobs, pay and postings are all healthy and layoffs are low, so a plain macro contraction does not fit. The rate-sensitivity story is the one worth watching — white-collar hiring is where the 2022 rate shock landed — but if rates were again the driver, the knowledge-work postings shortfall should be widening, and it is narrowing.

Finally, several panels that get talked about a lot contribute nothing here and I have not used them. AI systems now beat or tie human experts on about 71% of tested work tasks, and win outright just under half the time; the leading model can sustain tasks of roughly three hours at the measured reliability level. Adoption at 21.7% of firms — with 38.8% of large employers using AI in some function against 20.8% of the smallest — establishes only that the tools are in the building in sufficient numbers for a displacement story to be possible at all. It causes nothing by itself, and the bar for counting as an adopter is low.

What would move first if this is turning: the prime-age employment share. If it climbs back to flat or better against a year earlier while the long-term unemployed share retreats, the aggregate market is catching exits again and the displacement reading was wrong. That series publishes monthly, so there will be three more observations before the end of October.
